title: Effects and mechanism of CYBB on the progression of multiple sclerosis: Evidence from bioinformatic analysis and experimental validation
abstract: BackgroundNeutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are involved in the pathological progression of multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the intrinsic molecular mechanism by which NETs mediate the progression of MS remains unclear.MethodsDifferentially expressed genes were screened by integrating Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets and NETs-related genes, and candidate biomarker genes for MS were identified using machine learning algorithms and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.

title: A Solution-Processed Ti/Pt/NiOx/Ag RRAM Device with Multiple Forming-Free Non-Volatile Intermediate States
abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANN) implemented on crossbar arrays of non-volatile synaptic devices are known to consume much less energy compared to that implemented on conventional computing units. Solution-processed resistive random-access memory (RRAM) devices based on transition-metal oxides are suitable as such synaptic devices because of their cheap and easy fabrication method, stability, and suitable memristive properties. Here, in NiO-based RRAM devices with Ti/Pt as the bottom electrode and Ag as the top electrode (NiO layer deposited through solution processing), we experimentally report forming-free binary switching between a high resistance state (HRS) and a low resistance state (LRS) as well as forming-free pulse-driven modulation (long-term potentiation (LTP), long-term depression (LTD)) through 30 intermediate synaptic states between HRS and LRS (around 5-bit synaptic weight resolution). Many of these states are measured to be stable at least up to 1000 seconds confirming their non-volatility and their utility in storage of synaptic weights for ANN crossbar arrays. On the contrary, most prior experimental reports (including reports both on solution-processing-based and sputtering-based RRAM devices) require forming to exhibit non-volatility. Avoiding forming reduces variability, eliminates the need for high voltage pulses, and makes the crossbar array design simpler. Further, we confirm the presence of oxygen vacancies in our materials stack using X-ray photo-electron spectroscopy (XPS). Finally, we show successful data classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10 data sets using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model and a convolution neural network (CNN) model respectively, where the synaptic weight updates of these ANN models are calibrated against the experimentally measured LTP-LTD characteristics of the NiO RRAM devices.

title: Atoms that Matter: Largest Materials Datasets Are 99% Redundant, and Local Chemistry Can Guide the Required 1%
abstract: General-purpose machine-learning force fields (MLFFs) for materials are now trained on the order of $100$ million structures, assuming transferability requires such scale. We test this premise on OMat24, the largest available materials dataset, by training MACE models on subsets of $6.5$ million atoms, less than $1\%$ of OMat24, selected in three complementary ways: at random, by latent-space clustering of a pretrained MLFF (DIRECT), and by a new model-free method maximizing the diversity of discrete, interpretable local environments (EnvTok). All three models approach the full-data reference MACE-OMAT-0 model to within a few tens of $\mathrm{meV}/\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ in forces, and remain close to or exceed it on formation energies, elastic moduli, heat capacities, Li$^{+}$ migration barriers, and molecular-dynamics stability up to $3000\,$K and $500\,$GPa. This near-independence from the selection strategy shows that chemical environment diversity, not size, defines OMat24's information content: the remaining $99\%$ of structures are largely redundant. Broad sampling of chemical space thus remains essential, but reference labels are needed only for structurally and chemically distinct configurations. Using atomic positions and species, optionally augmented by magnetic moments, EnvTok identifies these before any labelling or training, yielding compact, architecture-independent datasets. This hundredfold reduction makes hybrid-DFT or higher-level relabelling of general-purpose training sets feasible, and frees computational budget for extending environmental coverage and multi-fidelity learning.

title: Cross-linker binding strength influences actin assembly microstructure and myosin II driven remodeling
abstract: The actin cytoskeleton is a self-assembled material that acts as the mechanical scaffold of the cell. Within the cell, protein cross-linkers organize actin filaments into assemblies with various microstructures that support distinct physiological functions. These protein cross-linkers differ in structural features. To decouple the role of individual cross-linker properties in actin assembly microstructure and mechanics, we synthesize programmable cross-linkers using a DNA linker coupled to binding domains. We find that high affinity cross-linkers induce actin bundling, while low affinity cross-linkers form actin networks. Myosin II motors remodel and contract all cross-linked networks tested in distinct ways from uncross-linked networks. We find that networks with high affinity cross-linkers have different myosin induced dynamics than networks with low affinity cross-linkers. This research expands our understanding of how cells regulate their mechanics and microstructures, while also providing insight towards the structure-property relationship in complex soft materials.

title: Comparative Analysis of Relative Ligand Binding Free Energy Simulation Methods: Amber-TI, GROMACS-NETI, OpenMM-FEP, and BLaDE-MSLD
abstract: Structure-based drug design has become increasingly important in the pharmaceutical industry for accelerating the discovery of effective drug candidates. In particular, ligand binding free energy serves as a critical metric for predicting drug efficacy during the key stages of hit discovery and lead optimization. Continuous progress has been made in the prediction of ligand binding free energies, but direct comparisons of different methods using the same force field remain challenging due to their unique implementations in different simulation engines. In this study, we present a direct comparison of four popular methodologies (Amber-TI, GROMACS-NETI, OpenMM-FEP, and BLaDE-MSLD) for calculating relative binding free energies (ΔΔGbind) with the same Amber protein and ligand force fields using MolCube Alchemical Free Energy Simulator (MolCube-AFES), which provides an input generation workflow to support ΔΔGbind calculations of all four methods. We used 80 alchemical transformations (among the JACS benchmark set by Wang et al.) and two additional applications to compare the predicted ΔΔGbind from the four methods against experimental measurements. All four methods reproduced experimentally observed trends, with most transformations within ±2 kcal/mol from experiments, and showed broadly comparable accuracy with no statistically significant performance differences across the benchmark data set. These results demonstrate that MolCube-AFES enables controlled, cross-platform benchmarking and show that all four different alchemical free energy methods deliver statistically equivalent accuracy, with method selection guided by workflow requirements such as throughput, portability, and perturbation network design rather than expected differences in performance.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: A modular mechanism determines the proton-pumping stoichiometry of respiratory complex I
abstract: Respiratory complex I, a crucial metabolic enzyme, uses the reducing potential of NADH to pump protons across energy-transducing membranes, but its mechanism of catalysis remains unknown. Here, guided by detailed structural information, we combine targeted mutagenesis and biophysical analyses to define the proton-pumping pathways in the three antiporter-like (proton-pumping) subunits of complex I from Paracoccus denitrificans and Escherichia coli. In Pd-CI, a four-proton pump, one of the three proton-uptake pathways is inactive, reconciling the four-proton/three-subunit mismatch. In Ec-CI two pathways are inactive - and Ec-CI pumps only two protons. We define the structural determinants for redox-coupled proton uptake, establish a mechanistic framework for proton pumping, and reveal how the proton-pumping stoichiometry has been adapted to deliver efficient energy conservation in diverse bioenergetic environments.

title: Systematic Analysis of GARP- and EARP-Mediated Trafficking Pathways Using Lysosomal Proteomics
abstract: Eukaryotic cells utilize tethering complexes for sorting of proteins within the endo-lysosomal system. The GARP complex and the EARP complex both function in endosomal recycling. Both complexes share three common subunits (VPS51, VPS52, and VPS53), with each relying on one specific subunit: VPS54 for GARP and VPS50 for EARP. Mutations in both complexes are linked to various neurodegenerative disorders. While model cargoes have been described, the cargo spectrum of both complexes remains largely elusive. Here, we combined lysosomal proteomics with knockdowns of GARP and EARP to analyze their cargo spectra. Using the lysosome as a terminal reference point for mis-sorted proteins, we show that GARP depletion causes a loss in lysosomal hydrolases and accumulation of non-lysosomal cargo. EARP depletion results in lysosomal accumulation of secreted proteins. Our findings serve as a reference to study GARP and EARP complexes. We demonstrate that a systematic phenotypic analysis of GARP and EARP mutants is necessary to understand the pathological consequences of their dysfunction.

title: Certified Design Regions under Parametric Plant Uncertainty with Application to Antithetic Integral Feedback
abstract: Kinetic parameters in engineered biomolecular circuits are typically known only within intervals and are not precisely tunable; controller synthesis is therefore naturally posed over sets of gains rather than at a single nominal design. We formulate robust controller tuning under parametric plant uncertainty as a universally quantified set-inversion problem: given a plant-parameter box, compute the controller gains that stabilize every plant in the box. Robust stability is decided by Hurwitz sign conditions, which are bounded over the joint gain-parameter domain using validated range enclosures, yielding machine-checkable certificates of local exponential stability of the deterministic equilibrium. Numerical experiments show that the certified region depends strongly on the range enclosure. For an antithetic integral feedback (AIF) controller acting on a two-species gene-expression cascade, a tensor-product Bernstein enclosure certifies 83.2% of the design plane at bisection tolerance epsilon=0.05 with 324 terminal boxes, whereas four baseline enclosures certify between 50.9% and 58.9% on the same paving. For a fifth-order loop, the certified fraction increases from 34.4% to 73.8%, and the certified and excluded terminal boxes confine the robustly stabilizing area to a window of about 2.1 percentage points. Finally, for a refining variant of the algorithm in which the plant box is refined alongside the design box, the undecided area satisfies |U(epsilon)|=O(epsilon) under a non-degeneracy assumption on the stability boundary.

title: High-throughput in vivo DNA data encoding by multiplexed conjugationand orthogonal base editing
abstract: Bacterial conjugation and CRISPR base editing offer complementary routes for programmable DNA transfer and heritable genomic writing, but their combined potential for information encoding in living cells remains unexplored. Here, we introduce CONCORD, a bacterial encoding platform that couples multiplexed bacterial conjugation to genomic base editing for synthesis-free in vivo DNA data writing. A recipient Writer strain expresses the base-editing machinery and is equipped with a writing template, whereas reusable donor Guide strains deliver the encoding sgRNA signals by conjugation.

title: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases synthesize DNA in a telomerase-like manner
abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) constitute an emerging class of bacterial defense systems that harness reverse-transcriptase activity to generate cDNA products and counter phage infection. A distinct subset of DRT10 systems evolutionarily related to telomerase generates tandem-repeat DNA to confer antiphage immunity. Here, we biochemically characterize the reverse transcription activity of DRT10 and determine cryo-EM structures of DRT10-ncRNA complex in three functional states, revealing an unanticipated 2:1 RT:ncRNA assembly mode. Two DRT10 protomers dimerize through a central pair of interlocked {beta}-hairpins and are further embraced by a single ncRNA. This architecture distinguishes DRT10 from previously characterized DRT complexes, which either lack an ncRNA component or exhibit an equivalent stoichiometry of RT:ncRNA. Strikingly, despite the nearly identical conformations of the two DRT10 protomers, cDNA product density was resolved in only one catalytic pocket, revealing different product occupancy within the dimer. Moreover, along with flanking linkers, the stem loops of the ncRNA as fixed points to supply steric barriers help define the template boundary. These findings reveal a distinctive ncRNA-mediated DRT10 dimeric assembly and establish a mechanistic framework for protein-primed reverse transcription constrained by the length of the RNA flanking linker.

title: Emergence of quantum transport in SnTe films upon structural refinement
abstract: Topological crystalline insulators are distinguished from the conventional Z2 topological insulators by crystalline symmetry protection of the surface states. Quantitative characterization of these states requires magneto-transport measurements from which the phase coherence length and number of independent coherent channels can be extracted. Here we report such measurements on textured thin films of SnTe grown on Bi2Te3 buffered c-plane sapphire (Al2O3) by pulsed laser ablation. A post deposition annealing protocol was implemented to control the crystallographic texture, which reveals improved crystallinity and enhanced epitaxial alignment along the [111] direction in films annealed at elevated temperatures. The higher carrier density and lower resistivity seen in films annealed at 100 oC are suggestive of Sn vacancies which act as native acceptor defects, while films annealed at 200 oC approach the 1:1 stoichiometry. The magnetoresistance of all samples at T 20 K, the MR is small and positive, and deviates from conventional Kohler scaling. An approximate collapse of the MR curves between 50 and 250 K is obtained using an empirical temperature-dependent scaling factor, indicating that changes in the Hall-derived carrier density alone cannot account for the observed scaling behavior. These results demonstrate that post growth annealing strongly influences the interplay between stoichiometry, crystallinity, and coherent transport in SnTe thin films.

title: UGME: A python package for non-Markovian protein folding dynamics
abstract: Biomolecular processes, including protein folding, protein-protein association, and protein-DNA recognition, often occur on timescales beyond what individual atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can reach. To access these longer-timescale dynamics, practitioners commonly combine many parallelized, short trajectories into reduced kinetic models, such as Markov state models (MSMs), that describe how the biomolecules interconvert between a handful of biomolecular configurations (e.g., folded and unfolded states of a protein). Central to MSM construction is the assumption that, at sufficiently long time lags, these projected dynamics become memoryless, such that the future evolution of the system depends only on its current state. Yet, projecting high-dimensional biomolecular dynamics onto a small set of states necessarily discards information about unresolved degrees of freedom, including solvent reorganization, side-chain rearrangements, and intermediate configurations. Because these unresolved motions can continue to influence subsequent dynamics, the resulting dynamics retain memory that is absent from a Markovian description. Here, we present ugme, a modular, open-source Python package for constructing and validating generalized master equations (GME) models that explicitly account for these non-Markovian (memory) effects.

title: Benchmarking machine-learning interatomic potentials using classical force fields
abstract: We propose a rational comparison between several well-known machine-learning interatomic potentials (linear atomic cluster expansion, the Behler-Parrinello high-dimensional neural network potential, and the graph neural network-based MACE potential) by testing their performance for fitting classical potentials such as the Lennard-Jones and Stillinger-Weber potential. With this we assess their advantages and limitations regarding several aspects: varying training dataset size, robustness to noise, carbon footprint, as well as the ability to reproduce the radial distribution function as an example observable. Overall the MACE models are shown to most accurately reproduce the potential energy surface, with little sign of overfitting, but at a significant computational cost, highlighting important questions regarding the choice of models in computational materials science.

title: Anisotropic pressure response of thermal conductivity in crystalline polytetrafluoroethylene
abstract: Compression can change thermal conductivity differently along polymer chains and across them by altering phonon velocities and lifetimes. We examine this directional response in orthorhombic Form III polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) at calculated pressures of 1.503, 3.452, and 5.056 GPa, using first-principles harmonic and cubic force constants within the single-mode relaxation-time approximation (SMRTA). At 100, 200, and 300 K, the chain-axis conductivity decreases at every pressure step. Between 3.452 and 5.056 GPa, both transverse components recover: at 300 K they increase by 23.7% and 13.7%, while the longitudinal conductivity decreases by 14.5%. An exact factorization separates the conductivity into a heat-capacity--velocity factor and a weighted effective lifetime. The transverse recovery follows from larger heat-capacity-weighted squared velocities, consistent with stiffer interchain restoring forces. Along the chains, shorter effective lifetimes dominate, and both conductivity-weighted Normal and Umklapp rates increase at 300 K. Comparing the same cubic force-constant blocks at all three pressures, we find that interchain coupling is already substantial at 1.503 GPa and increases under compression.

title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
abstract: Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests. Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT-report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734-0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645-0.736 for the next-best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759-0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703-0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets. Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology-enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state-of-the-art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining. We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR

title: Mn--Cr dopant association in dilute co-doped $\mathrm{ZnAl_2O_4}$ revealed by combined EPR and optical spectroscopy
abstract: Efficient and durable phosphors made from abundant elements underpin energy-saving solid-state lighting, near-infrared light sources for sensing, and X-ray and biomedical imaging. Co-doping is a standard route to brighter phosphors, yet the fate of the co-dopants is rarely established. We combine quantitative electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spin counting with photoluminescence, photoluminescence excitation, and X-ray-excited spectroscopy across two dilute Mn/Cr co-doping series of hydrothermally grown $\mathrm{ZnAl_2O_4}$ nanoparticles and show that the two ions can form an exchange-coupled, edge-sharing Cr--Mn defect complex, with $\mathrm{Mn^{2+/4+}}$ entering an octahedral site next to $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$. The octahedral Mn lifts the inversion symmetry of the $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ site and strengthens its parity-forbidden absorption, enhancing the $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ emission without energy transfer. The population of the defect complex follows the law of mass action, and above a threshold Mn concentration, Mn re-partitions into EPR-silent octahedral configurations that quench both emissions. Concentration optima in co-doped phosphors can thus reflect defect speciation, not only energy-transfer efficiency, which opens a structural design handle for brighter emitters.

title: Partitioning the magnetization raises the stability limit of ferromagnetic colloids
abstract: Magnetic actuation scales with a particle's magnetic moment, yet practical colloidal suspensions remain superparamagnetic or weakly magnetized, a permanent dipole drives a near contact attraction growing as the square of the moment, binding particles irreversibly. Here we show that this constraint depends not only on how much magnetic material a particle carries, but on where it sits. Partitioning a fixed moment M into N internal elements leaves the far field interaction, and every actuation force, unchanged while suppressing the near-field pair energy by 1/N. As we show in our experiments across 57 samples and three geometries, stability collapses onto a single $\sim M^{2}/N$ boundary, raising the accessible dipolar energy scale nearly 150-fold. A liquid-phase analogue of magnetic force microscopy images the engineered energy landscape directly. The resulting colloids outrun size-matched superparamagnetic beads in weak fields far from a magnetic source, suggesting their applicability in hard to reach places. Together, these results open a new operating regime for colloidal manipulation, with impactful implications in microfluidics and drug delivery.

title: Enhanced Aqueous-Phase Hydrodeoxygenation of Fatty Acids over CoP Anchored on P–N Co-Doped Carbon
abstract: The aqueous-phase hydrodeoxygenation of biomass-derived fatty acids offers an alternative route for the production of diesel-range hydrocarbons, but remains a major challenge. Herein, we report a hydrophobic CoP catalyst anchored on P–N co-doped carbon spheres (CoP@PNC-900), which exhibits high performance for the aqueous-phase hydrodeoxygenation of palmitic acid at 270 °C and 2 MPa H2, delivering nearly complete conversion together with over 99% yield of C15+C16 alkanes.

title: Decoupling Multi-Contrast Super-Resolution: Self-Supervised Implicit Re-Representation for Unpaired Cross-Modal Synthesis
abstract: Multi-contrast super-resolution (MCSR) is crucial for enhancing MRI but current deep learning methods are limited. They typically require large, paired low- and high-resolution (LR/HR) training datasets, which are scarce, and are trained for fixed upsampling scales. While recent self-supervised methods remove the paired data requirement, they fail to leverage valuable population-level priors. In this work, we propose a novel, decoupled MCSR framework that resolves both limitations.

title: Physics informed neural network framework for non-similar nano-heat and solutal transport in a rheological fluid over a stretching cylinder
abstract: Accurate prediction of non-similar momentum, thermal and solutal transport phenomena in rheological fluids is crucial for the design and optimization of advanced thermal management systems, heat exchangers, polymer processing, chemical reactors, energy conversion devices and biomedical transport processes. Motivated by these engineering applications, this study presents a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) framework for analyzing magnetohydrodynamic mixed convection flow of a Jeffrey fluid over a stretching horizontal cylinder embedded in a Darcy porous medium. The mathematical model incorporates the coupled effects of magnetic field, porous resistance, thermal radiation, Brownian diffusion, thermophoresis, viscous dissipation, velocity slip, internal heat generation, and Arrhenius activation energy along with chemical reaction. Owing to the non-similar nature of the governing equations, the Local Non-Similarity method is employed to transform the governing partial differential equations into a coupled system of ordinary differential equations, which is subsequently solved using a PINN implemented in PyTorch. The suggested algorithm is evaluated and tested with the help of BVP4C solver and shows good consistency with low [Formula: see text] error value of [Formula: see text] and stable convergence throughout the training phase. The results reveal that the rise in value of magnetic parameter reduce the velocity of fluid due to the Lorentz force while increase in Darcy number improves the flow due to decrease in porous effect. The thermal radiation and heat source have a major role to play in rising the temperature profile, while the increase in Schmidt number diminish the concentration distribution. The proposed LNS-PINN framework provides a computationally efficient procedure for simulating non-similar transport problems and offers a promising computational tool for engineering design and optimization of advanced systems.

title: In-Situ TEM Observation of Solid-State Phase Evolution in High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticles
abstract: The emergence of new materials has gone beyond conventional design principles. Among them are high entropy alloys (HEAs), in which multiple metallic elements coexist within a single unit cell. In this case, each atomic position in a solid material has a different chemical environment, leading to configurational entropy as high as that in the fully random or melted state, which has been frozen to a solid solution. However, the behaviour of such alloy systems at pre-melting temperatures is largely unknown, where atoms gain sufficient mobility and time to rearrange, leading to an enthalpic rather than an entropic interplay. This study demonstrated the phase transformation of HEA nanoclusters (CoCrFeMnNi) under high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at different temperatures, including room temperature (RT), 550 °C, and 850 °C. The clustered nanoparticles coarsen into larger clusters, accompanied by compositional heterogeneity due to surface and lattice diffusion. This experimental finding of atomic mobility was further corroborated using molecular dynamics, which provides a detailed mechanistic description.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems for Knowledge-Grounded Material Substitution
abstract: AI-assisted scientific discovery increasingly seeks to move beyond generating plausible ideas toward reproducible, constraint-aware workflows that can support practical engineering decisions. We present MARS, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning System for knowledge-grounded material substitution under scientific and manufacturing constraints. We apply MARS to replace per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a demanding materials-design problem in which substitutes must satisfy functional performance, environmental, experimental, and processing requirements. MARS decomposes substitution into a closed-loop workflow comprising requirement analysis, grounded candidate generation, and manufacturability assessment with process design. The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge-graph reasoning, a database of lab-available materials, persistent memory of intermediate results, and rejection-aware iterative feedback. In a PFAS-substitution case study, MARS generates structured material requirements, identifies an evidence-grounded substitute candidate, and develops a lab-scale manufacturing route. In a multi-seed ablation evaluation, MARS achieves the highest overall performance across all three subsystems, with gains that persist when the backbone model is held fixed. These results suggest that hierarchical decomposition, knowledge grounding, and manufacturability-aware refinement improve material-substitution reasoning beyond model capability alone.

title: Precursor stoichiometry controls dopant structure, defect chemistry, and valence in Mn-doped ZnGa$_2$O$_4$ nanocrystals
abstract: The luminescence of doped nanocrystals is usually optimised through the activator; here we show that the host cation ratio is an equally decisive, and largely overlooked, design variable. Mn-doped ZnGa$_2$O$_4$ nanocrystals (Mn:Zn = $4\times10^{-4}$) were grown hydrothermally at nominal Zn/Ga ratios between 0.30 and 0.75 (stoichiometric: 0.50) and post-annealed at 400--1100$^\circ$C, and the resulting composition--temperature matrix was mapped by X-ray- and UV-excited luminescence, EPR, Rietveld-refined X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy and SEM. The as-grown crystals are phase-pure spinel at every composition and accommodate their off-stoichiometry internally as a point-defect inventory, reflected in a 0.4\% variation of the lattice parameter; on annealing, the excess gallium is exsolved as $β$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ in amounts set by the solution composition. The Mn$^{2+}$ emission separates into two optima, near-stoichiometric crystals annealed at 400--600$^\circ$C and Zn-excess crystals annealed at 1100$^\circ$C, the latter being twice as bright under X-ray excitation. Under X-ray and 365~nm excitation the two optima are separated by a minimum at 800$^\circ$C that coincides with a collapse of the Mn$^{2+}$ EPR population and has no counterpart in the Raman linewidths, identifying transient, defect-compensated oxidation of the dopant rather than lattice degradation as its origin. The most Zn-rich composition shows neither Mn$^{2+}$ nor Mn$^{4+}$ emission at any annealing stage, whereas its trace Cr$^{3+}$ emission is strong, indicating that Mn is rejected already during growth. Solution stoichiometry therefore acts on two levels, dopant capture and native-defect inventory, while annealing controls dopant valence and lattice order. The brightest high-temperature phosphor is thus not the nominally stoichiometric one, but the composition whose excess is consumed on its way to stoichiometry.

title: Ground-State Phase Diagram of the Effective Model with Antiferromagnetic Nearest-Neighbor and Ferromagnetic Next-Nearest-Neighbor Interactions in 1/1 Periodic Approximants to Icosahedral Quasicrystals
abstract: By performing complete enumeration of all configurations of magnetic moments, we have determined the ground-state phase diagram of the effective model with antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interactions $J_1$ and ferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor interactions $J_2$ on the 1/1 periodic approximant to icosahedral quasicrystal. Depending on the ratio of $J_2/J_1$ and the magnetic anisotropy arising from the crystalline electric field, various non-collinear ferrimagnetic orders and antiferromagnetic orders are shown to be stabilized, whose magnetic space groups are identified as $R\bar{3}$, $C2'/m'$, $Pm'm'2$ and $I_{\rm P}m'\bar{3}'$. We have revealed the topological as well as magnetic property of each ground state with degeneracy, which is useful to understand experimental observations of magnetic structures and domains in the rare-earth-based 1/1 approximants.

title: Machine Learning in Amyloidogenic Polypeptide Research: From Sequence Prediction to Drug Discovery.
abstract: Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) has established a transformative paradigm for investigating amyloidogenic polypeptides. Characterized by their propensity to form ordered, β-sheet-rich fibrillar aggregates, these polypeptides are centrally implicated in the pathogenesis of numerous neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD).

title: Hamiltonian-Aware ADAPT Variational Quantum Eigensolver for Molecular Ground-State Simulation
abstract: Designing compact ansätze for the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is crucial for calculating energies of large molecules on near-term quantum devices. However, the widely used Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter (ADAPT) ansätze present two challenges: the inherent locality of conventional criteria results in inappropriate excitation operator selection, and the inevitable degradation of certain operators gives rise to redundant accumulation. In this paper, we propose the Hamiltonian-Aware (HA) ADAPT-VQE algorithm to address these issues.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Data-Driven Inference of Susceptibility, Correlation, and Dynamic Responses via Machine Learning
abstract: Understanding how complex systems respond to external perturbations is essential to characterize the intrinsic properties of the systems and then to control their responses. Despite some preliminary trials via either analytical modeling or numerical calculations, it is usually difficult to directly calculate the responses of complex systems (with high degrees of freedom) to strong perturbations.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Integrating machine learning failure probabilities and tracer-based infiltration indicators for sewer condition screening and asset management
abstract: Wastewater utilities need transparent decision-support methods to prioritise sewer rehabilitation when CCTV inspection data are incomplete and groundwater infiltration creates operational and environmental burdens. Machine learning (ML) models are being trained on sewer inspection data to perform as modern asset-management tools. However, given the limited availability of inspection data, independent external supporting data that are less resource-intensive to collect would be highly valuable. Tracer-based infiltration estimates are one such indicator.

title: Toward FOXM1 inhibitors based on supervised machine learning classification models and similarity-based screening
abstract: Ovarian cancer remains among the deadliest gynaecological malignancies, with aberrant activation of the Forkhead Box M1 (FOXM1) transcription factor strongly implicated in tumour progression, therapy resistance, and poor prognosis. Given the limited availability of validated FOXM1 inhibitors and the lack of prior dedicated machine learning-based QSAR studies identified in our literature survey, this study employed a supervised machine learning framework to predict the bioactivity of structurally diverse small-molecule inhibitors.

title: Synthesis and characterization of NIR fluorescent BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes
abstract: The development of NIR fluorescent dyes with favorable optical properties is of great importance especially for applications within the field of optical imaging. In this study, we report the design, synthesis and photophysical characterization of novel BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes obtained via Knoevenagel condensation between an asymmetrical BODIPY core and the functionalized xanthene aldehydes intermediates. The synthesized dyes ex-hibit absorption (667 nm) and emission bands (720-722 nm) within the NIR region.

title: Membrane Filtration Removes Lipids and Compromises the Acoustic Stability of Nanobubbles
abstract: Nanobubbles (NBs) have been widely investigated as ultrasound contrast and therapeutic agents, yet whether submicron gas bubbles can directly generate measurable ultrasound signals remains controversial. Because acoustic scattering scales with bubble size, several studies have recently attributed nanobubble echogenicity primarily to larger bubbles. A recent Science Advances publication, attributed the loss of ultrasound signal after filtration to the removal of residual larger bubbles [1]. This interpretation assumes that filtration acts solely as a size-selection process. Here, we show that filtration also alters the shell properties and stability of lipid-coated NBs, independent of size. Filtered NBs (F-NBs) show significant lipid loss and accumulation on the filters themselves, resulting in decreased bubble stability and greater susceptibility to destruction under acoustic excitation. To decouple size from processing effects, we generated NB populations size-matched to filtered samples using increased centrifugation (IC-NBs), a comparatively gentler separation method. Despite comparable size distributions, IC-NBs retained sustained ultrasound scattering, whereas filtered NBs showed significantly reduced acoustic persistence. Filtration through 5 m pores, ~5-fold larger than the largest bubbles, preserved acoustic persistence but still reduced bubble concentration by ~30%, suggesting that membrane contact may contribute to bubble loss beyond size exclusion. Complementary lipid and gas-content assays provided further evidence of filtration-induced changes. The 0.45 m filtration removed substantially more total lipid than could be attributed to free-lipid removal alone, while the lipid associated with the larger bubbles removed during filtration accounted for only ~5% of the additional lipid loss. Encapsulated gas content remained comparable to that of size-matched centrifuged controls, suggesting that the reduced acoustic stability of filtered NBs is more closely associated with changes in lipid content than with loss of the gas core. These results indicate that membrane filtration is not a purely size-selective process: it removes substantially more lipid than size exclusion predicts and yields bubbles that are less stable under ultrasound, most likely through changes in shell lipid content or in the surrounding lipid reservoir, underscoring the importance of processing-induced effects in interpreting nanobubble echogenicity.

title: Theory of exciton-exciton interactions with nontrivial electronic bands
abstract: Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs in semiconductors whose interactions influence optical properties and determine their collective behavior and emergent correlated phases. Despite the theoretical and experimental significance of these phenomena, a microscopic theory of exciton-exciton interactions that takes into account the full composite nature of these quasiparticles in systems with an arbitrary single-particle Hamiltonian is lacking. Here, we present a general theory of exciton-exciton interactions that builds upon our previous publication [Physical Review B 113, 155440 (2026)], which applied only to conventional semiconductors with weak band hybridization. By contrast, the theory presented here is valid in virtually any crystalline semiconducting system and can be applied to the study of biexciton formation and correlated excitonic phases in systems where band topology, quantum geometry, and moiré effects play a significant role. In addition to the analytical theory, we also present results in simple systems with flat bands with a nontrivial quantum metric and show that the biexcitonic spectrum differs strongly from that in the case without quantum geometry. Our theory paves the way for accurate quantitative calculations of biexciton spectra and excitonic many-body phases in modern condensed-matter systems.

title: Quantitative modeling of acid-base equilibria
abstract: Simulating acid-base equilibria from first principles is a tremendous challenge, as it requires modeling bond-breaking events in a complex hydrogen-bonding environment. The quantum mechanical behavior of the protons is often important, complicating simulations even further. We show that by combining state-of-the-art machine-learning potentials, accelerated sampling of the dissociation process, and an efficient estimation of nuclear quantum corrections it is possible to reliably compute the dissociation constants of different species in water. We demonstrate the transferability of this workflow, applying it successfully to the autoionization of water and to the entire ladder of the aqueous dissociation of phosphoric acid. The definition of the dissociation constant, the choice of order parameters, sampling artifacts and finite-size effects, as well as quantum nuclear effects all play a non-trivial role in determining the outcome of the calculation, so that cutting corners is likely to introduce biases that can only be compensated by fortuitous cancellations of errors.

title: Quantum dynamics of an ion in an RF quadrupole trap with weak octupolar anharmonicity
abstract: We investigate the quantum dynamics of a single ion confined in a radio-frequency (RF) Paul trap in the presence of weak octupole-induced anharmonicity, as can occur in realistic ion-trap potential. The explicitly time-dependent quadrupole potential is treated in a reference-oscillator Fock basis, allowing the effects of the RF drive and the quartic correction to be resolved directly at the level of motional-state couplings. While the quadratic RF interaction generates $Δn=\pm2$ transitions and Gaussian squeezing, the quartic contribution opens additional $Δn=\pm4$ coupling pathways. Starting from the reference-oscillator vacuum, we show that the octupole interaction broadens the even-parity Fock-state distribution and enhances the phonon-number fluctuations more strongly than the mean occupation. At the same time, the RF-induced sub-vacuum quadrature squeezing remains robust, although its magnitude and orientation are modified by the quartic interaction. The number statistics and quadrature fluctuations therefore respond differently to the same nonlinear perturbation, reflecting the distinct roles of Fock-space redistribution and phase coherence. The resulting dynamics provide a quantum-mechanical characterization of weak octupole corrections beyond the ideal quadrupole approximation and clarify how realistic anharmonicities modify nonclassical trapped-ion motion. Importantly, the motional nonclassicality remains robust against the weak octupole perturbation, as evidenced by persistent sub-vacuum quadrature squeezing and Klyshko-inequality violation. These results characterize how realistic anharmonic corrections reshape trapped-ion motion beyond the ideal quadrupole approximation.

title: Sample-efficient time-resolved X-ray crystallography with serial small wedges
abstract: Time-resolved crystallography can be inaccessible for membrane proteins and other difficult-to-crystallize targets for which suitable crystals are scarce. Here we present an acquisition strategy that records consecutive diffraction images during a small crystal rotation synchronized to a single activation pulse. Matching image segments are merged across crystals to reconstruct successive time windows, enabling a single crystal ensemble to capture an extended structural trajectory. Using the Mesh&Collect workflow at a synchrotron, we obtained ten consecutive 7.5-ms time windows at 2 [A] resolution from 1,255 microcrystals of a bacteriorhodopsin triple mutant at room temperature. An additional 790 crystals extended the observation window to 500 ms. Rotation-based processing, retrospective time binning and dose control maximize information extracted from each crystal, while compatible measurements can be pooled across acquisitions. This approach makes millisecond time-resolved crystallography practical for crystal-limited targets at synchrotrons, with further development potentially extending the temporal resolution down to 1 ms.

title: Copper-Catalyzed Chemo- and Enantioselective Radical 1,2-Carbosulfenylation of Diverse Alkenes with Broad Radical and Sulfur Compatibility
abstract: Enantioselective copper-catalyzed intermolecular radical 1,2-carbosulfenylation of alkenes with readily available alkyl halides provides efficient access to α-chiral alkyl organosulfur compounds, but its development has been hampered by competing side pathways and challenges in enantiocontrol. Herein, we report a general and versatile copper-catalyzed platform for chemo- and enantioselective radical 1,2-carbosulfenylation of a diverse range of alkenes.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Neural Network Prediction of Response Factors for Extractables and Leachables in Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices
abstract: Ensuring the safety of patients using pharmaceuticals and medical devices through chemical characterization requires accurate estimation of extractables and leachables to ensure tolerable risk from unintentional exposure to these chemicals. However, this is complicated by variability in chemical responses, particularly with mass spectrometry methods. High-quality relative response factor predictions provide the opportunity for both expedited and more accurate quantitation in extractables and leachables analyses.
venue: PDA journal of pharmaceutical science and technology

title: Masked Diffusion Language Agents for Tool-Integrated Chemical Reasoning
abstract: Designing tool-integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left-to-right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi-source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, enabling tool-use decisions to be jointly determined under full-trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary-order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two-stage post-training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine-tuning and variance-reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single-turn and multi-turn tool-use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.

title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
abstract: Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from. Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences. Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next. We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio. The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens. Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments. Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training-inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training, which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts. To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference. On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision. It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations. Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/.

title: MORAD: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Objective Rewards for RNA Inverse Design
abstract: We introduce MORAD, an online reinforcement learning framework for backbone-conditioned RNA diffusion models that trains a single shared policy across diverse target backbones. Structure-conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences compatible with a target three-dimensional backbone, yet existing reinforcement learning approaches either optimize a separate policy for each target backbone or rely on offline preference optimization, leaving online post-training of a reusable backbone-conditioned model largely unexplored. MORAD combines backbone-conditioned group sampling, group-relative reward normalization, and a forward-process diffusion objective. Beyond existing RL rewards that primarily target tertiary structural quality, MORAD jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition. To aggregate these heterogeneous objectives despite differences in scale and optimization direction, MORAD maps each measurement to a bounded desirability score and combines them with a weighted geometric mean. Compared with a tertiary-structure-only reward, this multi-objective formulation improves 10 of the 11 evaluation metrics that have a preferred direction. Applied to pretrained RIDE, MORAD improves GDT-TS by 16.0% (from 0.3300 to 0.3827) and pairing MCC by 19.4% (from 0.6110 to 0.7295), while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5% (from 0.3906 to 0.2830). On the test set, MORAD outperforms RiboDiffusion, gRNAde, and RDesign across tertiary structural accuracy, secondary-structure pairing, and thermodynamic quality, establishing a new state of the art in structure-conditioned RNA inverse design.

title: Proteome-guided drug discovery maps and mitigates therapeutic degrader toxicity
abstract: Heterobifunctional targeted degraders (HBDs) enable potent removal of protein targets but their clinical success can be hindered by de novo toxicity inherent to their bivalent chemistry. Here we introduce a drug discovery framework that exploits high-throughput proteomics to map and mitigate toxicity mechanisms of emerging drug modalities. Exposing androgen receptor (AR)-negative cells to a library of experimental AR-HBDs indicated for treatment-resistant prostate cancer linked widespread proteomic responses to hepatotoxicity of phthalimide degraders.

title: Frustration Quenching and Network Topology of the Energy Landscape as Primary Determinants of Protein-Ligand Binding Pose Prediction by Deep Learning Models
abstract: Deep learning co-folding and docking models accurately predict ligand binding poses at orthosteric sites yet systematically underperform at allosteric pockets. Here, we demonstrate that this accuracy gap reflects a fundamental biophysical property of local energy landscape topology specifically, the magnitude of frustration quenching upon ligand binding rather than an intrinsic algorithmic defect.

title: Closed-Loop CO2-Mediated Ultrafast and Controlled Synthesis of Amino Acid Polymers toward a Circular Carbon and Polymer Economy
abstract: The development of chemically recyclable polymers via net-zero CO2 emission is considered one of the ideal solutions to alleviate carbon imbalance and advance a circular polymer economy. Amino acid (AA) polymers, an important class of polyamides, provide an attractive molecular platform for constructing recyclable polymer systems. However, classical synthetic methods for AA polymers typically involve CO2 emissions and suffer from slow polymerization rate, poor controllability, and difficulty in achieving high molecular weight.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Identification of recycled PET fibers using TMAH-assisted reactive pyrolysis-GC/MS and machine learning
abstract: Recycled poly(ethylene terephthalate) (rPET) is increasingly used in polyester fibers, but reliable molecular-level identification remains challenging because chemical differences between virgin poly(ethylene terephthalate) (vPET) and rPET are often weak and distributed across multiple trace features. In this study, a tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH)-assisted reactive pyrolysis-gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (Py-GC/MS) workflow coupled with machine learning was developed to distinguish rPET from vPET fibers.

title: TopoLIA: Topology-Inspired Latent Interaction Attention for Drug Discovery
abstract: The growing sophistication of drug discovery calls for new advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Transformers have underpinned recent breakthroughs in AI, yet their conventional source-target attention mechanism can become a bottleneck for modeling complex interactions. Here, we introduce TopoLIA, a topology-inspired latent interaction attention mechanism that learns not only how much information should be exchanged between interaction partners, but also how that information should be transformed. Source-target-dependent attention is mediated through a compact latent interaction space, providing a structured representation of complex interactions. We further incorporate topological spectral representations to capture multiscale data geometry and extract algebraic relationships. TopoLIA thus incorporates topological principles into both data representation and neural network architecture. We demonstrate TopoLIA on protein-ligand binding, where persistent spectra encode multiscale topological and geometric patterns in 3D protein-ligand complexes, while latent interaction attention (LIA) enables structured, source-target-dependent information exchange. We pretrain TopoLIA by reconstructing masked multiscale spectral tokens from unlabeled molecular structures, yielding transferable structural representations without task-specific annotations. Across multiple scoring and docking benchmarks, TopoLIA achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently outperforms its standard-attention counterpart. Rank analyses show that compact latent dimensions yield the best performance, supporting compact interaction spaces as an effective inductive bias for biomolecular learning. More broadly, LIA provides a general framework for structured, source-target-dependent information exchange that is applicable to diverse scientific and AI problems involving complex heterogeneous interactions.

title: Mechanistic Study of a Thermal- and Light-Driven Single-Crystal-to-Single-Crystal Transformation of an Organocerium Complex
abstract: In crystallo synthetic and analytical methods are remarkably effective for stabilizing and structurally characterizing otherwise reactive compounds, and elucidating transient intermediates in catalytic cycles. In this work, we investigate the mechanism of the ring-opening isomerization of a CeIV-cyclopropenyl complex, CeIV(3,3-diphenylcyclopropenyl)(TriNOx) (Ce-1), to the corresponding CeIV-allenyl isomer, CeIV(CH═C═CPh2)(TriNOx) (Ce-2), where TriNOx3–═[((2-tBuNOH)C6H4CH2)3N]3–.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Birch-Type-Reduced Carbazole Anions Enable Redox-Adaptive Super-Reducing Photocatalysis
abstract: Photocatalytic activation of inert chemical bonds is constrained by the redox potential of the catalyst. Here, we report a redox-adaptive photocatalytic strategy in which an electron-rich carbazole photocatalyst, CBZ6, functions as a molecular redox transformer through the formation of Birch-type carbazole anions. Under visible light, CBZ6 switches between a neutral state for conventional photoredox reactions and an anionic state for super-reducing catalysis.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Wildfire smoke evolves as it drifts from wilderness to city
abstract: Faced with a warmer, smokier future, scientists work to understand the environmental and health risks of aged wildfire plumes

title: SSCHA-based evolutionary crystal structure prediction at finite temperatures with account for quantum nuclear motion
abstract: Reliable crystal structure prediction (CSP) at finite temperatures, including quantum anharmonic effects, remains challenging but is particularly important for systems containing light atoms such as superconducting hydrides. Here, we integrate machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) to enable evolutionary CSP on the quantum anharmonic free-energy landscape. Using LaH 10 as a test case, we compare three approaches: (i) active-learning MLIPs (AL-MLIPs) trained on the fly, (ii) universal MLIPs (uMLIPs), and (iii) temperature-dependent effective potentials (TDEPs) trained on SSCHA ensemble data. AL-MLIPs correctly predict the cubic Fm $$\bar{3}$$ 3 ¯ m phase but require thermodynamic perturbation theory corrections for consistent results. The foundation uMLIP Mattersim-5m enables SSCHA-based CSP without per-structure training, but fine-tuning is required for higher accuracy. Temperature-dependent effective potentials trained on SSCHA data enable accurate and very efficient CSP for large unit cells on the quantum anharmonic free-energy landscape. We demonstrate that quantum anharmonicity simplifies the free-energy landscape and is essential for the correct energy ranking of LaH 10 structures.

title: Grain Boundary-Confined Lead Halides Mitigate Post-Treatment Surface Lattice Distortion in Wide-Bandgap Perovskites for Efficient Tandem Solar Cells
abstract: Wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have attracted increasing attention due to their essential role in high-efficiency tandem architectures. Post-treatment strategies are commonly employed to improve WBG perovskite films by modifying surface states and enhancing device performance. However, such treatments risk simultaneously inducing surface lattice distortion, thereby undermining device efficiency. To address this issue, we strategically introduce lead thiocyanate into perovskite precursor solutions to induce the formation of excess lead halides at grain boundaries.

title: Hydrogen isotopes reveal water leakage from the core
abstract: Chemical heterogeneities in Earth's deep mantle may record either preserved primordial reservoirs or later core-mantle exchange, but distinguishing between these origins remains challenging. Hydrogen isotopes offer a sensitive tracer, yet whether magma ocean crystallization could generate a deuterium-depleted deep reservoir has not been quantitatively evaluated. Here, we use machine learning-accelerated path-integral simulations to determine equilibrium hydrogen isotope fractionation between silicate melt and bridgmanite, ringwoodite, and wadsleyite under magma ocean conditions. Incorporating these fractionation factors into a magma ocean crystallization model shows that mineral-melt fractionation is intrinsically weak, producing an essentially homogeneous D/H distribution in the primitive mantle. Magma ocean crystallization therefore cannot generate the extremely low δD values observed in some ocean island basalts. Combined with exceptionally high 3He/4He ratios, these signatures more plausibly reflect selective transfer of primordial volatiles from Earth's core, implying sustained volatile exchange across the core-mantle boundary.

title: Insights on the volume variation of LiCoxMn2-xO4 electrode upon cycling: a correlative operando XRD and XAS study
abstract: Understanding volume changes in high-voltage spinel cathodes is essential for mitigating mechanical degradation and improving cycling stability. However, linking these changes to cation-specific redox processes remains challenging. Here, we combine operando X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) to investigate the LiCoxMn2-xO4 spinel system, which exhibits a cubic structure and isotropic lattice response, in order to correlate the evolution of the local and long-range structure. Five compositions (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0) were synthesized and electrochemically characterized, with x = 0, 0.5, and 1.0 examined in detail under identical cycling conditions. XAS at the Mn and Co K-edges reveals distinct Mn4+/Mn3+ and Co4+/Co3+ redox processes, with Mn redox activity dominating below 4.7 V and Co redox triggered at higher potentials. Chemometric tools for XAS data analysis further resolve the evolution of local structure during cycling. Both XRD and XAS capture consistent trends in volume evolution, despite probing different structural length scales. Increasing Co content progressively decreases the overall volume change, from 5.0 % to 1.6 % by XAS and from 5.8 % to 2.1 % by XRD. These results demonstrate that Co substitution suppresses electrochemically induced structural strain and establish a direct link between cation-specific redox activity and volumetric evolution. The correlative operando XRD/XAS approach provides a framework to investigate newly designed low-strain, high-energy cathodes with improved cycling stability.

title: Assessing quantitative phase reliability in electron ptychography using a twisted trilayer WS2 thickness staircase
abstract: The phase of an electron wave is sensitive to the local electrostatic environment and can therefore provide information about atomic-scale structural variations. In electron ptychography, however, specimen thickness, multiple scattering and projected atomic overlap can complicate the quantitative interpretation of the reconstructed phase. Here, we use a twisted trilayer WS2 thickness staircase containing monolayer, bilayer and trilayer regions as an internal reference, with all regions measured under identical experimental conditions. The mean W-column phase increases by approximately 13.2% from the monolayer to the bilayer region, compared with only 4.7% from the bilayer to the trilayer region, revealing a nonlinear thickness dependence. W-S overlap has little effect on the W-column phase, whereas short-range projected W-W overlap increases it by approximately 8-9%. These results provide a benchmark for evaluating quantitative phase measurement in multilayer WS2 and for assessing phase-based mapping of local electrostatic potential, charge-density and three-dimensional atomic-scale polarization.

title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual-use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess hazardous knowledge possession rather than practical application, overlook risk amplification from BDTs, and rely on unreliable, expensive, or hazardous validation methods. To address these gaps, we introduce DRYLAB-Bench (Design Risk Yielded by LLM Agent in Biodesign), the first comprehensive benchmark evaluating the high-risk biological mutation design capabilities of LLM agents. Moving beyond basic question-answering, DRYLAB-Bench tasks agents with 30 genuinely hazardous mutation-design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines. It evaluates models in a multi-round, tool-augmented environment where LLMs orchestrate BDTs to iteratively refine candidates. Crucially, it scores designs directly against 187,695 empirical wet-lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using our proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS), quantifying risk-associated effects while enabling scalable and safe ground-truth verification. Evaluations of 15 frontier models reveal substantial baseline threats: without tools, 67.6% of one-shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest-risk decile. Equipping models with BDTs significantly amplifies this risk, raising the pooled risk by \(ΔBRS=+0.116\) and the top-decile share to 23.5%. Code: https://github.com/drylab-bio/DRYLAB-Bench

title: Role of composition-tuned disorder on magnetic exchange interactions in NiRuMnGa
abstract: We report the experimental investigation of the quaternary Heusler alloy NiRuMnGa, complemented by first-principles calculations. The energetically favorable crystal structure was identified from first-principles calculations and subsequently used as the structural model for refinement of the powder X-ray diffraction data. The refinement shows good agreement with the experimental pattern and reveals substantial B2-type disorder involving Ni/Ru and Mn/Ga site intermixing. The dc magnetic response exhibits pronounced ZFC--FC irreversibility near $\sim 48$ K, with the irreversibility temperature shifting toward lower temperatures under increasing magnetic field, indicating a field-sensitive glassy state. The isothermal magnetization remains unsaturated up to 7 T, reaching only $\sim 0.4\,μ_{\mathrm{B}}$/f.u., accompanied by pronounced hysteresis, suggesting competing exchange interactions and frustrated magnetic moments. AC susceptibility, together with magnetic relaxation and memory measurements, confirms slow spin dynamics characteristic of a cluster glass state. The lack of a discernible heat-capacity anomaly near the irreversibility temperature further supports the absence of conventional long-range magnetic order. Collectively, these results demonstrate that competition between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions in NiRuMnGa leads to magnetic frustration and stabilizes a cluster glass state.

title: Scaling RNA Foundation Models through Iterative Refinement
abstract: Biological function in RNA is encoded across scales, from local sequence motifs to long-range structural dependencies. Conventional RNA foundation models couple parameter capacity and inference depth within a fixed architecture, prescribing a fixed computation graph for each inference. Here we present Eco-RNA, an 80M-parameter RNA foundation model that makes inference depth adjustable through learned iterative refinement. Its shared, input-conditioned Transformer core refines sequence representations through repeated application. The iteration count is selected after training and controls effective depth at fixed model parameters. We train across recurrent depths with masked reconstruction, state regularization, and a one-sided loss that anchors deeper reconstruction to a shallow reference. On the 70-assay RNAGym fitness benchmark, increasing refinement from one to four iterations raises aggregate absolute Spearman correlation from 0.242 to 0.286, with the gain retained through eight iterations. At four iterations, Eco-RNA surpasses the current SOTA Evo 2 40B on all three aggregate fitness metrics despite 500x fewer parameters. Its iteration configurations advance the compute-performance Pareto frontier among the evaluated models. It also outperforms the evaluated baselines in non-coding RNA family classification, RNA secondary-structure prediction, and chemical probing profile prediction. These results establish internal inference computation as an effective scaling dimension for RNA foundation models.

title: Metabolic immune checkpoints (MICs) in cancer: from molecular mechanisms to challenges and opportunities in clinical translation
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a core feature of tumor cells in adapting to microenvironmental stress and acquiring malignant phenotypes. It not only supports rapid proliferation but also mediates immune escape by reshaping the immune microenvironment. In recent years, the "metabolism-immune axis", serving as a central hub for the crosstalk between metabolic regulation and immune suppression, has provided a new perspective for understanding tumor immune evasion. This review systematically discusses how metabolic pathways, including glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism, along with mitochondrial function and other related processes, shape the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment by regulating immune cell function, immune checkpoint expression, and immune signaling networks, thereby promoting tumor immune escape. The concept of "metabolic immune checkpoints (MICs)" is innovatively proposed and classified into three categories based on their mechanisms of action: (1) MIC-I: metabolic modification-type immune checkpoints, exemplified by posttranslational modifications of immune checkpoint molecules such as PD-L1 lactylation, acetylation and glycosylation, etc.; (2) MIC-II: metabolic enzyme-dependent immune regulatory nodes, represented by enzymes such as indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 and others that directly influence immune cell function; and (3) MIC-III: microbial metabolite-coupled immune regulatory targets, including receptors for microbe-derived metabolites such as short-chain fatty acid receptors. By integrating molecular interaction networks of key targets such as lactate dehydrogenase A and ATP citrate lyase, this review explores synergistic therapeutic strategies that combine small-molecule inhibitors targeting MICs with immune checkpoint blockade. This highlights how metabolic intervention can restore immune cell function and reverse exhaustion. Current key challenges in clinical translation include limitations in metabolic dynamic monitoring technologies, lack of patient stratification biomarkers and insufficient specificity in microbiome regulation. Future directions will focus on personalized treatment guided by multiomics, integrating single-cell metabolic flux analysis, deep learning-driven target prediction, and synthetic microbiome engineering, driving tumor immunotherapy into the era of precision metabolic regulation. By integrating the fundamental mechanisms of MICs with translational medical research, this review not only provides a systematic paradigm but also establishes a foundation for the development of new-generation precision combination therapies.

title: Electron- and hole-doped superconductivity in two-dimensional electride ZrX$_2$ (X = Cl, Br, I)
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) superconducting systems have recently emerged as a frontier in condensed matter physics, driven by their unique physical properties and potential applications. Using first-principles calculations, we show that monolayer ZrX$_2$ (X = Cl, Br, I), which is a family of 2D semiconducting electrides, hosts phonon-mediated superconductivity under both electron and hole dopings. Electron doping in ZrX$_{2}$ can achieve high superconducting transition temperatures at very low concentrations, with ZrBr$_2$ reaching $T_c = 30.0$ K at 0.01 \textit{e}/f.u., followed by ZrCl$_2$ (22.5 K at 0.05 \textit{e}/f.u.) and ZrI$_2$ (18.1 K at 0.01 \textit{e}/f.u.), for which the high $T_c$ originates from the flat conduction band minimum, with Van Hove singularities nearby enhancing the density of states. In contrast, hole doping requires higher concentrations (0.2--0.25 \textit{h}/f.u.) to activate superconductivity, yielding $T_c \sim 2$ K, and approaches a magnetic instability at elevated doping levels. By comparing with InSe and LaBr$_2$, we identify the spatial location and orbital character of excess electrons as key factors determining the strength of hole-doped superconductivity and the nature of competing orders. These findings establish monolayer ZrX$_2$ as a platform for bipolar superconductivity in a 2D electride and provide insights into flat-band engineering for high-$T_c$ superconductors.

title: X-ray absorption spectroscopic studies of oxygen-deficient double perovskite oxide NdBaCo$_2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim 0.65$)
abstract: The degree of oxygen vacancy in A-site-doped layered double perovskite oxides can lead to anion vacancy ordering, which subsequently results in distinct superstructures. We have studied oxygen deficient double perovskite oxide, NdBaCo$2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim$ 0.65), utilising X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy complemented by multiple scattering and first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT+U). The present results establish a direct correlation between oxygen-vacancy distribution, magnetic inhomogeneity, and charge transport in layered cobaltates. Our investigations on the Co K, Ba, and Nd $L_{\mathrm{III}}$ edges suggest that the near-edge spectra, based on the number and shape of the spectral features, indicate the value of $δ$ for the compound under study lies closer to 0.75. The analysis of the Ba $L_{\mathrm{III}}$ edge spectrum confirms the +2 oxidation state for Ba ions. The Co K-edge near-edge spectra suggest the possibility of oxygen vacancies arising at the basal sites in addition to the apical sites. This is counterintuitive to the common understanding that oxygen vacancies usually occur at the apical sites, i.e., in the lanthanide (Nd) layer in these compounds. Such a distribution of oxygen vacancies naturally explains the Griffith phase and the conduction mechanism of variable range hopping observed in the compound. The vacancy distribution, when at the optimum level, can also bring about easier oxygen ion mobility and a more sensitive and faster oxygen sensor. We believe that our results will help in tailoring oxygen-ion mobility and enhancing oxygen-sensing performance.

title: Orbital transfer reveals material-selective structure in Rydberg excitons
abstract: Rydberg excitons in atomically thin semiconductors offer a sensitive view of dielectric screening and electronic structure. As their spectra become increasingly well resolved, a central question is how much material information an effective Hamiltonian can predict beyond the states used to determine it. Using the 1s, 2p and 2s levels to determine a scalar Rytova-Keldysh Hamiltonian, we test its transfer to the excluded 3p state. The transfer deviations have opposite signs: the observed 3p lies 7.38 meV below the prediction in MoSe2 and 5.58 meV above it in WS2; the opposite signs persist across the complete reported +/-2-sigma peak-error boxes. In a separate high-field-calibrated benchmark, RK removes 66.8% of the orbital error of a pure two-dimensional Coulomb reference, making the remaining state-selective deviations particularly informative. After separating gap and common-scale contributions, the residuals reveal distinct material-dependent orbital patterns and constrain simple multichannel descriptions. For WS2, the measured 2p/3p curvatures yield a parameter-fixed prediction, Q4p=+4.08 meV, for a future same-platform measurement. Together these results show how a well-performing spectral model can be tested for transferable physical information, with the next unmeasured state providing an independent experimental check.

title: Myelin Sheath-Inspired Fluorocarbon Hydrophobic Bridges for Stable n-Type Organic Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductors
abstract: Operationally stable n-type organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) remain a critical bottleneck for organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) for application in bioelectronic and neuromorphic devices. However, several state-of-the-art n-type OMIECs suffer from performance decay and poor stability when operated in aqueous media. Inspired by myelin sheaths, we challenge the conventional “π-backbone + hydrophilic side-chain” design and propose a molecular architecture with fluorocarbon hydrophobic bridges to spatially segregate, at the molecular level, ionic and electronic pathways. By tuning the fluorocarbon bridge chain length in fluorocarbon-ethylene glycol chain substituents [−CH2(CF2)nCH2(OCH2CH2)5OMe = 2nFG; n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6] of a DPP-CNTVT polymer series (2nFG-P), we balance electron transport, ion exchange, redox chemistry efficiency, and water incorporation. Extensive in situ spectroelectrochemistry, EIS, Raman, EQCM-D, AFM, and GIWAXS characterization reveals that tuning the length of the hydrophobic bridge enables good electron transport, suppresses excessive water incorporation, and enhances stability. Thus, the polymer with a mid-length bridge, 8FG-P (n = 4), achieves the greatest electron transport (μC* ∼ 157 F cm–1 V–1 s–1, μ ∼ 1.22 cm2 V–1 s–1), fastest response (τon/τoff = 2.6/1.5 ms), and retains >90% of the initial performance after 10,000 s of operation in water, a result independent of the polymer molecular weight. This strategy potentially expands OMIECs design principles and offers useful insights toward stable n-type OECT semiconductors.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Modeling centrosome positioning by actin--microtubule crosstalk and actin anchoring at the cell membrane
abstract: Centrosome positioning is governed by mechanical interactions between the actin and microtubule cytoskeletons, yet the contribution of different actin architectures and their attachment to the cell membrane remains unclear. We use numerical simulations to study a centrosomal array of microtubules interacting with cortical, bulk, and centrosome-associated actin networks, including passive cross-linkers, motor proteins, and ERM-mediated coupling of actin to the cell membrane. We find that bulk and centrosome-associated actin alone are insufficient for robust centrosome centering, whereas sufficiently dense cortical actin promotes centering through steric interactions with growing microtubules. ERM-mediated attachment of cortical actin to the cell membrane enhances this effect, allowing stable centering at lower actin densities. In a two-centrosome system, microtubule interactions generate a spindle-like structure, while the organization of actin and its membrane attachment through ERM regulate centrosome separation. Antagonistic microtubule motors further limit centrosome separation and establish a finite spindle length.
